one_liner: Promise-based MD5 for Node and browsers with a hand-written WAT core; about 39x faster than md5 npm on 37 MB.
what_it_does: md5WASM(data) takes a Buffer, ArrayBuffer or Uint8Array and returns a Promise that resolves to the hex MD5 string. It ships as one dependency-free JavaScript file (about 26 KB) with the WebAssembly module embedded as base64, exported for CommonJS, AMD and window.md5WASM. It is not a drop-in for the md5 npm package: strings must be converted to bytes first, there is no synchronous or incremental (streaming) API, and inputs above 268,369,920 bytes (255.9 MB) are rejected.
how_it_is_fast: The core is a hand-written WebAssembly text module (four-logics-syntax.wat) whose loops() export runs the 64 MD5 steps over 61,440 consecutive 64-byte blocks (3.75 MiB) per call, reading message words straight from linear memory with i32.load and keeping the A-D state in wasm globals, so no JavaScript number conversions happen inside the loop (the README's explanation for the gap). Input bytes are packed into a Uint32Array view of the wasm memory, and whatever the wasm chunks do not cover is finished by a hand-unrolled JavaScript MD5 over that typed array. Much of the advantage over the md5 npm package comes from this better-written JavaScript as well: the rows where no WebAssembly runs are still 1.3-8.3x faster than md5 (derived from page data).
when_to_use: MD5 checksums of multi-megabyte buffers (well above 4 MiB) in a browser, where Node's crypto module is not available, e.g. hashing a user-selected video before upload.
Replacing the md5 npm package in legacy code that hashes large Buffers or Uint8Arrays and can accept a Promise-based call.
When a single MIT-licensed file with no dependencies and no build step is preferred over a larger hashing library.
when_not_to_use: In Node.js: the built-in crypto.createHash('md5') (native OpenSSL) is the obvious incumbent and was never compared.

Inputs up to about 4 MiB: no WebAssembly runs (see gotchas), and an independent run at 1 MiB measured md5-wasm's JS path at 131.77 MB/s versus 171.73 MB/s for pure-JS spark-md5 3.0.2 and 850.31 MB/s for hash-wasm 4.10.0 (Chrome 131, Ryzen 9 7900X).
Streaming or chunked hashing of files larger than memory, or inputs over 255.9 MB: the whole input must be in one buffer and is copied into a fresh wasm memory.

Latency-sensitive UI or server threads: the hash is computed synchronously on the calling thread despite the Promise API, and each WebAssembly call recompiles the module (about 150 ms on the author's server).
Code that passes strings or needs a synchronous result (issue #3 asked for synchronous support; none was added).

integration.form: source-drop (single JS file with base64-embedded wasm; npm package md5-wasm 2.0.0)
integration.min_toolchain: A JavaScript engine with WebAssembly and Promise (falls back to JavaScript with a console message if WebAssembly is missing); README numbers from Node v10.18.1
integration.thread_safety: Each call builds its own closures, WebAssembly.Memory and instance, so concurrent calls are independent (a multiple-simultaneous-calls bug was fixed in May 2020 per the commit log); hashing itself runs synchronously on the calling thread.

gotchas: Unit mismatch behind the README table: md5WASM sends inputs larger than 1,048,576 bytes down the WebAssembly path, but md5WA only calls the wasm loops() while more than 1,048,576 32-bit words (4 MiB) remain, since len and i count words. Inputs from 1 MiB to about 4 MiB therefore compile the module, allocate wasm memory and copy the data, then hash entirely in JavaScript, and on larger inputs the last 0.25-4 MiB is always hashed in JavaScript. The README's 0.2-2 MB rows ran no WebAssembly at all; the same thresholds are in npm 1.0.2, 1.1.0 and the current file.

'Non-blocking' describes only the API shape: the JavaScript path hashes inside the Promise executor before md5WASM returns, and the WebAssembly path hashes synchronously in the instantiate callback. Every WebAssembly-path call recompiles the module from bytes and allocates at least 512 wasm pages (32 MiB) of memory, up to 4,096 pages (256 MiB) for the largest inputs.

The README table is a set of single runs committed 2020-05-02, before the May 2020 WebAssembly optimisation and the v2.0.0 rewrite (Feb 2021). Its small rows are non-monotonic (0.2 MB 90 ms, 0.3 MB 300 ms, 0.5 MB 360 ms, 1 MB 170 ms), which points to cold-JIT noise, and it names no CPU and ships no benchmark script.

The only independent numbers (hash-wasm README, via hash-wasm-benchmark's md5.worker.js) time md5-wasm at 32 B and exactly 1 MiB, both on its pure-JS path: 6.1x over md5 2.3.0 at 1 MiB (derived from page data), but slower than spark-md5 and 6.5x slower than hash-wasm's compiled-C WebAssembly MD5.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the sibling hashes (superfasthash, sha2-wasm, tape-sha256) computes MD5, so the real choice is against hash-wasm, which is already in this wave's merged records and measured 6.5x faster at 1 MiB, or spark-md5. Pick md5-wasm only for large in-memory buffers where a tiny dependency-free file matters more than peak speed.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README table (Node v10.18.1, unnamed low-powered Ubuntu server, single runs, no script): MD5 of a 37 MB file takes 990 ms versus 38,500 ms with the md5 npm package (37 vs 0.96 MB/s, about 39x), falling to 1.3-2.9x on the 0.2-0.5 MB rows, where only JavaScript runs. An independent hash-wasm benchmark (Chrome 131, Ryzen 9 7900X) puts md5-wasm 2.0.0 at 131.77 MB/s versus 21.65 MB/s for md5 2.3.0 at 1 MiB, on its JavaScript fallback.
status_note: The code has been frozen since v2.0.0 (February 2021); later commits only touch the README or are housekeeping (the 2026-04-23 commit is 'Fighting with git'), and there are no tests (the npm test script is a stub). It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but the speedup is overstated for inputs under about 4 MiB because of the byte/word threshold mismatch.
